127.title: A chapter a day
127.hook: most Bible-reading habits are small: one chapter, same time, every day
127.howItsDone: Many Christians read a chapter or a set passage of the Bible every day, often with a reading plan, a daily devotional or the church's lectionary, at a regular time such as early morning or before bed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two testaments, and your line: the story began long before. Did you read the six verses of Psalm 1? Today, how people actually keep reading. Day one hundred twenty-seven.

January first. A fresh start, and a big resolution: this is the year I read the whole Bible, cover to cover. You start at Genesis. Creation, the flood, Abraham, Joseph: it's great. Exodus: plagues, the sea splitting, even better. Then, around February, you reach Leviticus. Chapter after chapter of rules for sacrifices, skin diseases and mildew. And somewhere in there, the bookmark stops moving. If that's happened to you, you're in very large company. Here's what people who've read the Bible for decades tend to say: the grand plan isn't what lasts. What lasts is small. One chapter. Same time. Same chair. Every day. Today's word is that habit.
screen: `THIS IS THE YEAR.` → `LEVITICUS, AROUND FEBRUARY.` → `THE BOOKMARK STOPS.`

segments.voice: A chapter a day. The idea is old. In the book of Acts, the people of a town called Berea are praised because they "searched the scriptures daily." Daily. Not in one heroic weekend. God tells Joshua, "thou shalt meditate therein day and night." A little, often. Here's some math. The Protestant Bible has about eleven hundred and eighty-nine chapters. At one a day, that's a little over three years for the whole thing. Most chapters take three or four minutes to read. About as long as this lesson. Here's a surprise: chapters aren't original. The biblical writers didn't use them. The chapter divisions most Bibles use were added in the thirteenth century, and verse numbers came even later, in the 1500s. They're handles, not part of the text. Christians have built all kinds of plans on those handles. A Scottish minister in 1842 made a plan that took his congregation through the whole Bible in a year, at four chapters a day. The Book of Common Prayer takes Anglicans through all hundred and fifty psalms every month. Catholics hear scripture on a set cycle of readings at every daily Mass, and many Protestants use reading plans on their phones. And if you're starting from nothing, many pastors and priests give the same advice: don't start at Genesis. Start with a Gospel. Mark is the shortest, sixteen chapters. Sixteen days, and you've read a whole account of the life of Jesus. Missed a day? The plan doesn't care. Pick it up where you left off. Small and daily wins.
screen: `THEY SEARCHED THE SCRIPTURES DAILY.` · `ABOUT THREE YEARS, ONE A DAY.` · `CHAPTERS CAME LATER.` · `START WITH MARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your time and your place. Settle, and breathe. Picture your ordinary day. Where is there four minutes that's already yours? Morning coffee. The bus. Lunch. Right before bed. Pick one. Now pick the place: a chair, a corner, a seat on the train. See yourself there with a Bible, or an app, open to Mark, chapter one. If you pray, you can offer that time to God before it starts. If you don't, simply decide it's yours. The bell holds the time.
A chapter a day. The small, steady habit most lifelong Bible readers keep: one chapter, same time, every day. Today's word.
Your line: small and daily wins. Today, read one chapter at the time and place you chose. Mark chapter one is a good door. Day one hundred twenty-seven.

128.title: A lamp for my feet (Psalm 119:105)
128.hook: people memorize a verse to carry it in the dark
128.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize Bible verses, often starting in childhood Sunday school, and repeat them in hard moments; Psalm 119:105 is one of the most commonly memorized.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a chapter a day, and your line: small and daily wins. Did you read your chapter in your chosen spot? Today, something even smaller: one verse, carried. Day one hundred twenty-eight.

Have you ever walked down a dark path at night with only your phone's flashlight? A camping trip, a power cut, a country road. The light doesn't show you the whole way. It shows you the next two steps. A root. A puddle. The edge of the path. And that turns out to be enough. You keep walking, two steps at a time. Now picture an older kind of light: a little clay oil lamp, small enough to hold in your palm, with a wick and a tiny flame. In ancient Israel, that's what you'd carry at night. It didn't light up the road ahead. It lit your feet. Today's word is a verse written by someone who knew exactly what that felt like.
screen: `A PHONE FLASHLIGHT ON A DARK PATH.` → `THE NEXT TWO STEPS.` → `A CLAY LAMP IN YOUR PALM.`

segments.voice: Here it is, from Psalm 119, in the King James Bible: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." A lamp for my feet. Not a floodlight. Not a map of the next ten years. Enough light for the next step. That's the promise the psalm is making about God's word: not that you'll see everything, but that you won't walk blind. Psalm 119 itself is remarkable. It's the longest chapter in the entire Bible, a hundred and seventy-six verses. And it's built like a puzzle. In Hebrew it's an alphabet poem: twenty-two sections, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and in each section all eight verses begin with that letter. Our verse opens the section for the letter nun, and the Hebrew word for lamp, ner, starts with it. Almost every verse in the psalm mentions God's word in some form: law, statutes, precepts, commandments. Someone was in love with it. Earlier in the same psalm is a line that explains why people memorize verses at all: "Thy word have I hid in mine heart." Hid, as in stored away. Christians, and Jews with their own psalms, have always done this. A verse learned by heart goes where a book can't: into a hospital bed, a prison cell, a sleepless night, a moment when there's no phone and no light. People who've lost almost everything, their memory, their sight, sometimes still have the verses they learned as children. A verse carried is a lamp you don't have to find in the dark.
screen: `NOT A FLOODLIGHT: THE NEXT STEP.` · `176 VERSES, AN ALPHABET POEM.` · `THY WORD HAVE I HID IN MINE HEART.` · `A LAMP YOU CARRY INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn the verse by heart. Settle, and breathe. Say the first half, slowly: thy word is a lamp unto my feet. Again. Once more, with your eyes closed. Now the second half: and a light unto my path. Again. Now put them together, the whole verse, three times. Don't rush. Let each phrase land on a breath. If you pray, you can make it a prayer. If you don't, just let it settle in. Keep repeating it quietly until the bell. The bell holds the time.
screen: `THY WORD IS A LAMP UNTO MY FEET, AND A LIGHT UNTO MY PATH.`

129.title: Reading slowly
129.hook: reading for information and reading for formation are different speeds
129.howItsDone: Many Christians read scripture slowly, often aloud or under their breath, repeating a phrase and pausing on a word; monks and nuns practice this daily as lectio divina, and many Protestants read a single verse slowly in a morning quiet time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a lamp for my feet, and your line: a lamp unto my feet. Can you still say the whole verse? Try it now, in your head. Today, the speed you read at. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

Think about how you read the terms and conditions on a new app. You don't. You scroll to the bottom and hit agree. Now think about how you'd read a letter from someone you love who has died, found in a drawer years later. You'd read it slowly. You'd stop at a phrase. You'd read it again. You might read one sentence ten times and hear their voice in it. Same eyes, same brain, same alphabet. Completely different reading. Most of us read everything at the first speed now: headlines, feeds, emails, skimming for what we need. Christians have long said the Bible is meant to be read, at least sometimes, at the second speed. Today's word is that second speed.
screen: `TERMS AND CONDITIONS: SCROLL, AGREE.` → `A LETTER FOUND IN A DRAWER.` → `TWO SPEEDS OF READING.`

segments.voice: Reading slowly. Some Christian writers call the two speeds reading for information and reading for formation. The first asks: what does this say? The second asks: what is this doing to me? Both matter. You need the first to know what's there. But the second is where the words start to shape a life. The Bible itself describes the slow kind. The first psalm praises the person whose "delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night." That word meditate, in Hebrew hagah, doesn't mean sitting silent with an empty mind. It means to murmur, to mutter under your breath. Isaiah uses the same word for a lion growling over its prey. Picture it: someone going over the words out loud, again and again, low and slow, like a lion that won't let go. In the ancient world, almost all reading was out loud. Augustine, in his Confessions, tells how surprised he was to see the bishop Ambrose reading with his eyes moving and his voice silent. Medieval monks called slow reading rumination: chewing on the words the way a cow chews the cud. You met their method on day one hundred one, lectio divina: read, notice a word, ponder, rest. Christians of every church read this way in some form. Monks and nuns. Protestants with a single verse in a morning quiet time. People who imagine themselves into a Gospel scene. The pace is the point. At full speed, the words pass through you. Slowed down, one word can stop you in your tracks.
screen: `INFORMATION, THEN FORMATION.` · `HAGAH: TO MURMUR.` · `A LION THAT WON'T LET GO.` · `ONE WORD CAN STOP YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read five lines at half speed. If you have a Bible, open to Psalm 23 and read the first five verses. If not, use its first line: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." Settle, and breathe. Read it once, at normal speed. Then again, twice as slowly, murmuring it under your breath. Let one word catch you, and stop there. Say it again. Don't rush to the end. If you pray, you can let that word become your prayer. If you don't, just stay with it. The bell holds the time.
screen: `THE LORD IS MY SHEPHERD; I SHALL NOT WANT.`

segments.voice: Reading slowly. Reading for formation, not only information: murmuring the words until one stops you. Today's word.
Your line: slow down to hear. Today, read one thing twice as slowly as usual, a verse, a letter, a message from a friend, and notice what you hear. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

130.title: Tyndale's plow
130.hook: Tyndale died so a ploughboy could read the Bible in English; many translations followed, KJV and Douay-Rheims among them
130.howItsDone: Christians read the Bible in many translations; Protestants often use versions descended from Tyndale and the King James, Catholics use approved Catholic translations descended from the Douay-Rheims tradition, and Bible societies of many churches work to translate it into every language.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading slowly, and your line: slow down to hear. What stopped you when you slowed down? Today, the last of ten days on sabbath and scripture: how those words reached English at all. Day one hundred thirty.

England, the 1520s. A young scholar named William Tyndale, who reads Greek and Hebrew, gets into an argument with a churchman. The story goes that Tyndale told him, if God spared his life, he'd see to it that a boy who drives the plow would know more of the scriptures than he did. Translating the Bible into English without church permission was forbidden. So Tyndale left England for good. In Germany, in 1526, he printed a New Testament in English, small enough to hide. Copies were smuggled across the sea in bales of cloth, and many were burned. Nine years later, he was betrayed and arrested in Antwerp, and in 1536, near Brussels, he was strangled and his body burned. The story is that he died praying that God would open the king of England's eyes. Today's word is what he gave his life for.
screen: `A BOY WHO DRIVES THE PLOW.` → `SMUGGLED IN BALES OF CLOTH.` → `ARRESTED, STRANGLED, BURNED.`

segments.voice: Translation. From the Latin for carried across. Every Bible in English is a carrying-across, from Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek. Before Tyndale, followers of John Wycliffe had copied English Bibles by hand, translated from Latin. Tyndale went back to the original languages, and he had an ear. He gave English words and phrases it still uses: Passover. Scapegoat. Let there be light. The salt of the earth. When the King James Bible appeared in 1611, its New Testament leaned heavily on Tyndale's wording. Scholars estimate that most of it is his. So when you've heard the King James quoted on this path, you've often been hearing Tyndale. English Catholics made their own translation too, in exile in France, from the Latin: the Rheims New Testament in 1582 and the Douai Old Testament decades later. That's the Douay-Rheims, the Catholic Bible in English for centuries. It's honest to say this was a violent age on every side. Protestants and Catholics were both put to death for their faith in those years. Thomas More, who wrote fiercely against Tyndale, was himself executed by Henry the Eighth a year before Tyndale died. Christians of every church remember their own martyrs from that time. But here's what nearly all Christians share now: the conviction that anyone should be able to read the Bible in their own language. Today it has been translated in full into hundreds of languages, and in part into thousands more. Every one of them cost someone years, and some of them cost a life. Looking back on these ten days: rest, the Lord's Day, a library, two testaments, a chapter, a lamp, slowness, and now the price of the words.
screen: `TRANSLATION: CARRIED ACROSS.` · `PASSOVER, SCAPEGOAT, LET THERE BE LIGHT.` · `KING JAMES AND DOUAY-RHEIMS.` · `A VIOLENT AGE ON EVERY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember who taught you to read. Settle, and breathe. Go back. A parent with a picture book. A first-grade teacher. An older sibling. A librarian. Someone who sat beside you and pointed at letters until they became words. See their face if you can. Think about what that one gift has opened for you since. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. If you don't, just let yourself feel grateful. If they're still alive, decide how you might tell them. The bell holds the time.
Translation. From the Latin for carried across. The work that brought the Bible from Hebrew and Greek into English, at great cost. Today's word.
Your line: words cost someone something. Today, thank someone who taught you to read, or teach someone something with words. Tomorrow, a new stretch: giving and singing. Day one hundred thirty.

131.title: The tithe (Malachi 3:10)
131.hook: many Christians give a tenth; others give differently, but most give regularly
131.howItsDone: Many Christians give regularly to their church and to the poor; some tithe ten percent of their income, while others give a proportion they decide themselves, often through a weekly offering or a regular automatic gift.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tyndale and translation, and your line: words cost someone something. Did you thank someone who taught you to read? That closed sabbath and scripture. Now a new stretch: giving and singing. Day one hundred thirty-one.

Payday. The money lands in your account, and within minutes it's already spoken for: rent, groceries, the phone bill, the car, the thing you promised your kid. Whatever's left at the end of the month is what's left. Most of us live that way. Now go back almost four thousand years, in the story, to Abram, the man who'll become Abraham. He's just come back from a battle, and a mysterious priest-king named Melchizedek comes out to meet him with bread and wine, and blesses him. And Abram's response is simple. In the King James words: "And he gave him tithes of all." A tenth of everything. Off the top. Before anything else. It's the first time the idea appears in the Bible. Today's word is that tenth.
screen: `PAYDAY, ALREADY SPOKEN FOR.` → `ABRAM AND MELCHIZEDEK.` → `A TENTH, OFF THE TOP.`

segments.voice: Tithe. It's an old English word meaning a tenth. In the Hebrew scriptures, tithes of grain, wine, oil and flocks supported the priests and Levites who served at the sanctuary, and some went to the poor: the widow, the orphan and the stranger. It was worship and welfare in one. The most famous line comes from the prophet Malachi, speaking to people who had stopped giving: "Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing." Christians today read that verse in different ways. Many evangelical and Pentecostal churches teach tithing as a standard: ten percent of income, given to the local church. Many Catholic, Orthodox and mainline Protestant churches teach generous, regular giving without a fixed number, and point to Paul: "every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." Some preachers read Malachi as a promise that giving will make you rich; many other Christians strongly disagree with that reading. What most Christians share is the idea of firstfruits. Proverbs says to honor God with the first of your harvest, not the leftovers. The point isn't the math. It's the order. When giving comes first, it shapes everything after it. When it comes last, there's usually nothing left.
screen: `TITHE: A TENTH.` · `WORSHIP AND WELFARE IN ONE.` · `A TENTH, OR A CHEERFUL GIVER.` · `FIRSTFRUITS, NOT LEFTOVERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: decide one regular gift. Settle, and breathe. Think about something you care about: a church, a food bank, a neighbor, a cause. Now think of one small, regular gift you could give it. It can be money: an amount so small it doesn't scare you. It can be time: an hour a month. It can be a skill. Don't decide the whole plan. Decide the first gift, and when it happens. If you pray, you can offer it to God before it leaves your hands. If you don't, simply choose it freely. The bell holds the time.
Tithe. A tenth: the old practice of giving the first part of what you have to God and to those in need. Today's word.
Your line: give first, not last. Today, set up your one regular gift, however small, so it goes out before everything else. Day one hundred thirty-one.

132.title: Two small coins (Luke 21:1–4)
132.hook: a widow drops in almost nothing, and Jesus says she gave the most
132.howItsDone: Christians often speak of the widow's mite when they talk about giving: many churches teach that a gift is measured by its cost to the giver rather than its size, and some also read the story as a call to protect the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tithe, and your line: give first, not last. Did you set up your one small gift? Today, a gift so small it barely made a sound. Day one hundred thirty-two.

The temple in Jerusalem, a few days before the cross. Jesus is sitting across from the treasury, where people bring their offerings, and he's watching. Wealthy people come by, one after another, and drop in their gifts. Big gifts. You can almost hear the weight of them. Then a widow walks up. In that world, a widow often had no income, no property and no one to speak for her. She has two tiny copper coins, the smallest money there was. She drops them in. Nobody would notice. Nobody would thank her. Except that Jesus calls his disciples over and says: see her? She gave more than all of them. Today's word is what she put in.
screen: `WATCHING THE TREASURY.` → `BIG GIFTS, ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` → `A WIDOW, TWO COPPER COINS.`

segments.voice: Two small coins. The King James calls them "two mites." In Greek, each is a lepton, which means something small and thin: the tiniest copper coin in use. Mark's Gospel says two of them made a single quadrans, a Roman coin worth a fraction of a day's wage. Next to nothing. Here's what Jesus says, in Luke: "Of a truth I say unto you, that this poor widow hath cast in more than they all: For all these have of their abundance cast in unto the offerings of God: but she of her penury hath cast in all the living that she had." Jesus is doing different math. He doesn't count what went into the box. He counts what was left behind. The rich gave from what they had extra. She gave what she had to live on. Measured by cost, she gave the most. Christians have read this story for centuries as a picture of wholehearted giving: it's not the amount, it's the heart and the cost. But notice where Luke places it. Just before, Jesus warns about religious leaders who, in the King James words, "devour widows' houses." Just after, he says the temple itself will be torn down. So some scholars hear a second note: not only praise for her, but grief that a system would take a poor widow's last coins. Churches hold both readings. One asks what our giving costs us. The other asks what our institutions cost the poor. Either way, Jesus sees the person nobody else was watching.
screen: `LEPTON: SMALL AND THIN.` · `SHE HATH CAST IN MORE THAN THEY ALL.` · `COUNT WHAT WAS LEFT BEHIND.` · `PRAISE, AND A LAMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a gift that costs you. Settle, and breathe. Not the easy gift, the extra you won't miss. Think about what's actually precious to you right now. Maybe it's time: an evening you'd been guarding. Maybe it's attention: listening to someone who tires you out. Maybe it's something you own and love. Choose one small thing that would really cost you, and one person or place to give it to. If you pray, you can offer it to God, the way she did. If you don't, just notice what giving it would mean. The bell holds the time.
Two small coins. The widow's gift of two tiny copper coins, all she had to live on: the least money and, Jesus said, the most given. Today's word.
Your line: it's not the amount. Today, give the one thing you chose, something that costs you, however small. Day one hundred thirty-two.

133.title: Give in secret (Matthew 6:1–4)
133.hook: don't let your left hand know what your right hand is doing
133.howItsDone: Many Christians give to the poor quietly, through unsigned gifts, anonymous envelopes or church funds that keep donors' names private, taking Jesus's words about secret giving as their guide.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two small coins: a widow dropped in almost nothing, and Jesus said she gave the most. Your line was it's not the amount. What did you give that actually cost you something? Day one hundred thirty-three.

Think of the last time you did something kind and nobody saw. Maybe you paid for the coffee behind you. Maybe you picked up the trash in the stairwell. And be honest: did some small part of you want someone to find out? A tiny wish that it would come up in conversation, or that the person would turn around just in time to see it was you? That wish is so human it's almost funny. Everyone has it. And Jesus, in the middle of the Sermon on the Mount, reaches right in and puts his finger on it. He pictures a man giving to the poor with a trumpet blowing in front of him. Today's word is the old name for that gift.
screen: `A KINDNESS NOBODY SAW.` → `DID YOU WANT THEM TO?` → `A TRUMPET IN FRONT OF THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Alms. It's an old English word for gifts to the poor, and it has traveled a long way. It comes, through Latin, from the Greek eleēmosynē, which grows out of eleos, mercy. So alms are mercy you can hold in your hand. The same root sits in the old church cry Kyrie eleison: Lord, have mercy. Now the passage, in Matthew chapter six. Jesus doesn't say whether to give. He takes that for granted. He talks about how. The King James Bible puts it like this: "when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do." Nobody is sure whether anyone ever literally blew a trumpet. Some readers think it's a picture, a joke even, like saying don't toot your own horn. Others connect it to the trumpet-shaped offering boxes said to stand in the Temple. Either way, the point lands. People who give for applause, Jesus says, get the applause, and that's all they get. Then the strangest line: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." You can't actually hide something from your own hand. That's the point. He's asking for a gift so quiet that even you barely make a story out of it. "That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly." Christians have taken this seriously for centuries: the anonymous envelope, the unsigned check, the groceries left on a porch. Jews have a long tradition here too; the medieval teacher Maimonides ranked a gift where giver and receiver don't know each other near the very top. The idea underneath is freeing. A secret gift is the only kind you can't use to buy anything back.
screen: `ALMS — MERCY YOU CAN HOLD.` · `NO TRUMPET BEFORE THEE.` · `THE LEFT HAND DOESN'T KNOW.` · `A GIFT THAT BUYS NOTHING BACK.` · then, large: `THY FATHER WHICH SEETH IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle and breathe. Somewhere this week, there's a gift you could give that nobody will trace back to you. A few dollars in a jar. A kind review for a small business, unsigned. A bill paid quietly for someone who's short. Let one come to mind. Don't plan how it will feel when they find out, because they won't. Notice the small tug to tell someone. Let it pass. If you pray, you can offer the gift to God, who sees in secret. If you don't, just let it be yours alone. The bell holds the time.
Alms. Gifts to the poor, from a Greek word rooted in mercy. Jesus asks for them quietly, without the trumpet.
Your line: let it stay secret. Sometime this week, give something anonymously, and then tell no one, not even the group chat. Day one hundred thirty-three.
